sectionTitle: Energy changes in a system, and the ways energy is stored before and after such changes — part 4.1.1.2

specStatements.text: Students should be able to calculate the amount of energy associated with a moving object, a stretched spring and an object raised above ground level.
The kinetic energy of a moving object can be calculated using the equation:
kinetic energy = 0.5 × mass × (speed)^2
kinetic energy, Ek, in joules, J
mass, m, in kilograms, kg
speed, v, in metres per second, m/s
The amount of elastic potential energy stored in a stretched spring can be calculated using the equation:
elastic potential energy = 0.5 × spring constant × (extension)^2
(assuming the limit of proportionality has not been exceeded)
elastic potential energy, Ee, in joules, J
spring constant, k, in newtons per metre, N/m
extension, e, in metres, m
The amount of gravitational potential energy gained by an object raised above ground level can be calculated using the equation:
g.p.e. = mass × gravitational field strength × height
[E_p = m g h]
gravitational potential energy, Ep, in joules, J
mass, m, in kilograms, kg
gravitational field strength, g, in newtons per kilogram, N/kg (In any calculation the value of the gravitational field strength (g) will be given).
height, h, in metres, m

scopeNotes.statement: (assuming the limit of proportionality has not been exceeded)
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every elastic potential energy calculation in this content states that the spring is within its limit of proportionality, and the one question that goes beyond the limit asks only that the equation can no longer be used. No content asks students to calculate the energy stored in a spring stretched past its limit of proportionality, and no alternative equation is offered for that case.

scopeNotes.statement: In any calculation the value of the gravitational field strength (g) will be given.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every gravitational potential energy calculation states the value of g in the question itself, and no item requires students to recall a value. One question makes the provision explicit by asking where the value of g comes from.

concepts.definition: The energy an object has because it is moving. For an object of mass m moving at speed v it is calculated from kinetic energy = 0.5 × mass × (speed)², that is Ek = 1/2 m v². This equation must be recalled.

concepts.term: Quantities in the kinetic energy equation
concepts.definition: In Ek = 1/2 m v² the kinetic energy Ek is in joules, J; the mass m is in kilograms, kg; and the speed v is in metres per second, m/s. Substituting values in any other units gives an answer that is not in joules.
The quantity measured in kilograms, kg, that appears in both Ek = 1/2 m v² and Ep = m g h. It is not the same as weight, which is a force measured in newtons.
The speed of the moving object, in metres per second, m/s. In the kinetic energy equation the speed is squared, so kinetic energy changes far more quickly than speed does.

The energy stored in a stretched spring. It is calculated from elastic potential energy = 0.5 × spring constant × (extension)², that is Ee = 1/2 k e², assuming the limit of proportionality has not been exceeded.
The quantity in the elastic potential energy equation, measured in newtons per metre, N/m. A larger spring constant means a stiffer spring, so more energy is stored for the same extension.

The increase in the length of the spring beyond its unstretched length, measured in metres, m. It is not the total stretched length of the spring, and it must be converted from centimetres or millimetres before use.
The point beyond which the extension of a spring is no longer proportional to the force applied. Ee = 1/2 k e² gives the energy stored only while the limit of proportionality has not been exceeded.

The energy gained by an object raised above ground level, calculated from g.p.e. = mass × gravitational field strength × height, that is Ep = m g h, with Ep in joules, J. This equation must be recalled.
The quantity in the g.p.e. equation, measured in newtons per kilogram, N/kg. In any calculation the value of the gravitational field strength will be given in the question.
The vertical height through which the object is raised above ground level, in metres, m. It is the vertical rise, not the distance moved along a slope or ramp.
The unit of energy. Kinetic energy, elastic potential energy and gravitational potential energy are all measured in joules, J.

Because speed is squared in Ek = 1/2 m v², doubling the speed makes the kinetic energy four times greater. Because extension is squared in Ee = 1/2 k e², doubling the extension makes the stored energy four times greater. Height is not squared in Ep = m g h, so doubling the height only doubles the g.p.e.
Ek = 1/2 m v² and Ep = m g h are equations that must be recalled. Ee = 1/2 k e² is provided on the Physics equations sheet. Knowing which is which affects how each is revised, not how it is used.

Before substituting into these equations, mass must be in kilograms (divide grams by 1000) and extension and height must be in metres (divide centimetres by 100). Substituting grams or centimetres gives an answer that is wrong by a factor of 1000, 100 or 10 000.

misconceptions.question: A car of mass 1200 kg travels at 10 m/s. What is its kinetic energy?
misconceptions.misconception: You work out 0.5 × mass × speed, so 0.5 × 1200 × 10 = 6000 J.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The equation is often remembered as the words 'half m v', and the small squared symbol is dropped when the equation is written from memory under time pressure.
misconceptions.correction: The equation is kinetic energy = 0.5 × mass × (speed)². Square the speed first, then multiply by the mass and by 0.5. Writing 0.5 × 1200 × (10 × 10) makes the order clear.

misconceptions.question: A cyclist doubles their speed. What happens to their kinetic energy?
misconceptions.correct: It becomes four times greater, because the speed is squared.
misconceptions.misconception: If the speed doubles, the kinetic energy doubles too.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Most everyday relationships students meet are directly proportional, so doubling one quantity is assumed to double the other. The squared term is not noticed.
misconceptions.correction: Ek = 1/2 m v², so doubling v multiplies (speed)² by 2² = 4. Check it with numbers: 1/2 × 60 × 4² = 480 J, but 1/2 × 60 × 8² = 1920 J, which is four times as much.

misconceptions.question: In Ek = 1/2 m v², which quantity is squared?
misconceptions.correct: The speed, v, is squared. The mass is not.
misconceptions.misconception: The mass is the one that gets squared, so you work out 0.5 × (mass)² × speed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In the written form 1/2 m v² the small 2 sits at the end of a string of symbols, and students who do not read it carefully attach it to whichever quantity they meet first.
misconceptions.correction: The index belongs only to the symbol it is written after, so v² means the speed is squared. The word form makes it unambiguous: kinetic energy = 0.5 × mass × (speed)².

misconceptions.question: A spring of spring constant 50 N/m is extended by 20 cm. How much elastic potential energy is stored?
misconceptions.correct: Convert first: e = 0.20 m, so Ee = 0.5 × 50 × 0.20² = 1 J.
misconceptions.misconception: You can put 20 straight into the equation, giving 0.5 × 50 × 20² = 10 000 J.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The number in the question is 20, and students substitute the number they are given without checking that the unit matches the one the equation requires.
misconceptions.correction: The extension e must be in metres. 20 cm = 0.20 m. Because the extension is squared, using centimetres makes the answer 10 000 times too large.

misconceptions.question: A spring 8 cm long is stretched until it is 12 cm long. What value of e is used in Ee = 1/2 k e²?
misconceptions.correct: e is the extension, 12 cm - 8 cm = 4 cm = 0.04 m.
misconceptions.misconception: e is the length of the stretched spring, so e = 12 cm = 0.12 m.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The symbol e is read as standing for the spring itself rather than for the change in its length, and the stretched length is the more obvious number in the question.
misconceptions.correction: Extension means the increase in length from the unstretched length, so subtract the original length first.

misconceptions.question: A spring is stretched beyond its limit of proportionality. Can Ee = 1/2 k e² still be used?
misconceptions.correct: No. The equation gives the energy stored only while the limit of proportionality has not been exceeded.
misconceptions.misconception: The equation is the equation, so it works for any extension you like.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Equations are treated as universal rules, and the bracketed condition in the specification looks like a footnote rather than part of the equation.
misconceptions.correction: Beyond the limit of proportionality the extension is no longer proportional to the force, so there is no single spring constant that describes the spring and the equation no longer applies.

misconceptions.question: A box is pushed 5.0 m up a ramp that rises 2.0 m vertically. Which distance is h in Ep = m g h?
misconceptions.correct: h is the vertical rise, 2.0 m.
misconceptions.misconception: h is the distance the box actually moved, 5.0 m along the ramp.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The 5.0 m is the distance the object travels, and students transfer the habit from work done = force × distance, where the distance moved along the line of action is the one that is used.
misconceptions.correction: In Ep = m g h, h is the height raised above ground level, measured vertically. The route taken does not change the g.p.e. gained.

misconceptions.question: An object weighs 500 N where g = 10 N/kg. What value goes in as m in Ep = m g h?
misconceptions.correct: The mass, m = 500 / 10 = 50 kg.
misconceptions.misconception: You use 500 as the mass, because that is the number the question gives for how heavy it is.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday language 'weight' and 'mass' are used for the same idea, and both are stated as a single number describing how heavy something is.
misconceptions.correction: Mass is in kilograms and weight is a force in newtons. Weight = mass × gravitational field strength, so divide the weight by g to get the mass before using Ep = m g h.

misconceptions.question: A ball of mass 250 g moves at 4 m/s. What is its kinetic energy?
misconceptions.correct: Convert first: m = 0.25 kg, so Ek = 0.5 × 0.25 × 4² = 2 J.
misconceptions.misconception: You substitute 250 for the mass, giving 0.5 × 250 × 4² = 2000 J.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Grams are the more familiar everyday unit, and the number given in the question is substituted without conversion.
misconceptions.correction: The mass m must be in kilograms. 250 g = 0.25 kg. Using grams makes the answer 1000 times too large.

misconceptions.question: What is the unit of the spring constant, k?
misconceptions.correct: Newtons per metre, N/m.
misconceptions.misconception: Newtons per kilogram, N/kg, the same as gravitational field strength.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both constants are written as a lower-case letter and both are newtons per something, so the two units are stored together and then swapped.
misconceptions.correction: The spring constant is newtons per metre, N/m, because it tells you the force per metre of extension. Gravitational field strength is newtons per kilogram, N/kg, because it is the force per kilogram of mass.

misconceptions.question: What is the unit of kinetic energy?
misconceptions.correct: The joule, J.
misconceptions.misconception: The newton, because that is the unit you use in physics for how much push something has.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Energy and force are both loosely described as how much something can do, and the newton is the unit met most often in mechanics.
misconceptions.correction: All three energy stores in this section are measured in joules, J. The newton is the unit of force.

misconceptions.question: Which equation gives gravitational potential energy?
misconceptions.correct: g.p.e. = mass × gravitational field strength × height.
misconceptions.misconception: It must be 0.5 × mass × gravitational field strength × height, because the other two energy equations start with 0.5.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Two of the three equations in this section begin with 0.5, so the pattern is generalised to the third.
misconceptions.correction: Ep = m g h has no factor of 0.5. Only the kinetic energy and elastic potential energy equations, where a quantity is squared, carry the 0.5.

misconceptions.question: Where does the value of g come from in a g.p.e. calculation?
misconceptions.correct: It is given in the question.
misconceptions.misconception: You have to remember it, and it is always 10 N/kg.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Textbook questions use a familiar value so often that it starts to look like a constant students are expected to memorise.
misconceptions.correction: In any calculation the value of the gravitational field strength (g) will be given, and the value supplied in the question is the one to use.

misconceptions.question: A spring of spring constant 200 N/m is extended by 0.10 m. How much energy is stored?
misconceptions.misconception: You work out 0.5 × 200 × 0.10 = 10 J.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The equation is recalled as 'a half k e' and the squared term on the extension is dropped, especially as it is the equation students meet least often.
misconceptions.correction: The extension is squared: elastic potential energy = 0.5 × spring constant × (extension)². Square the extension before multiplying.

misconceptions.question: A load is raised twice as high as before. How does the g.p.e. gained change?
misconceptions.correct: It doubles, because height is not squared in Ep = m g h.
misconceptions.misconception: It becomes four times greater, in the same way that doubling speed makes kinetic energy four times greater.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The squared relationship is learned so firmly from the kinetic energy equation that it is applied to the g.p.e. equation as well.
misconceptions.correction: In Ep = m g h the height appears to the power one, so g.p.e. is directly proportional to height. Doubling h doubles Ep.

misconceptions.question: Object A has mass 4 kg and speed 3 m/s. Object B has mass 2 kg and speed 6 m/s. Which has more kinetic energy?
misconceptions.correct: B does: Ek(A) = 18 J and Ek(B) = 36 J.
misconceptions.misconception: They must be the same, because 4 × 3 and 2 × 6 both give 12.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students compare the product of mass and speed, which is equal here, without noticing that only the speed is squared.
misconceptions.correction: Square the speed first. Ek(A) = 0.5 × 4 × 3² = 18 J and Ek(B) = 0.5 × 2 × 6² = 36 J, so halving the mass but doubling the speed doubles the kinetic energy.

misconceptions.question: A spring has been stretched past its limit of proportionality. How should the stored energy be found?
misconceptions.correct: Ee = 1/2 k e² cannot be used for it.
misconceptions.misconception: You can still use the equation as long as you change the spring constant to a new value.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know something about the spring has changed, and assume the fix is to update the constant rather than to abandon the equation.
misconceptions.correction: Past the limit of proportionality the force is no longer proportional to the extension, so the spring has no single spring constant and the equation does not apply.

misconceptions.question: Why is there a 0.5 in kinetic energy = 0.5 × mass × (speed)²?
misconceptions.correct: It is part of the equation and must always be included.
misconceptions.misconception: The 0.5 is a small correction, so leaving it out only changes the answer a little.
misconceptions.whyItArises: A factor of one half looks like a rounding adjustment rather than an essential part of an equation, particularly when answers are quoted to a couple of significant figures.
misconceptions.correction: Omitting the 0.5 doubles the answer, which is a 100% error. Both Ek = 1/2 m v² and Ee = 1/2 k e² require it.

misconceptions.question: A light object moving quickly and a heavy object moving slowly: which stores more kinetic energy?
misconceptions.correct: It must be calculated, and speed counts for more because it is squared.
misconceptions.misconception: The heavier one always stores more energy, because kinetic energy is really about how heavy something is.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday experience says that heavy things are harder to stop, so mass is treated as the quantity that decides the answer.
misconceptions.correction: Both mass and speed appear in Ek = 1/2 m v², but only the speed is squared, so a change in speed affects the kinetic energy far more than the same fractional change in mass.

misconceptions.question: Is energy measured in watts?
misconceptions.correct: No. Energy is measured in joules, J.
misconceptions.misconception: Watts and joules both measure energy, so either unit will do.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Watts are met alongside joules on appliance labels and in energy questions, and the difference between energy and the rate of transferring it is easily lost.
misconceptions.correction: The joule is the unit of energy. The watt is the unit of power, the rate of energy transfer.

misconceptions.question: What does the spring constant tell you?
misconceptions.correct: The force needed per metre of extension, in N/m.
misconceptions.misconception: The energy stored per metre of extension, so its unit is joules per metre.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The spring constant is met inside an energy equation, so it is assumed to be an energy quantity.
misconceptions.correction: The spring constant relates force to extension, so it is measured in newtons per metre, N/m. The energy stored is what you calculate from it using Ee = 1/2 k e².

misconceptions.question: What is the unit of gravitational field strength in this equation?
misconceptions.correct: Newtons per kilogram, N/kg.
misconceptions.misconception: Something with metres and seconds in it, because gravity is about how fast things fall.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Falling motion is the most familiar context for gravity, so units of motion are reached for instead of the unit of a field strength.
misconceptions.correction: In Ep = m g h the gravitational field strength g is in newtons per kilogram, N/kg: the gravitational force acting on each kilogram of mass.

misconceptions.question: A 20 kg box is raised 2.0 m where g = 10 N/kg. How much g.p.e. does it gain?
misconceptions.misconception: You multiply the mass by the height, giving 20 × 2.0 = 40 J, because gravity is just the reason it gains energy.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Gravitational field strength is read as a description of the situation rather than as a number that has to be multiplied in, especially when it is given separately from the other data.
misconceptions.correction: All three quantities are multiplied together: g.p.e. = mass × gravitational field strength × height. Leaving g out makes the answer ten times too small when g = 10 N/kg.

misconceptions.question: Does raising an object more slowly change the g.p.e. it gains?
misconceptions.correct: No. Ep = m g h depends only on the mass, the field strength and the height.
misconceptions.misconception: Lifting it faster gives it more gravitational potential energy.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Effort and speed feel connected in everyday lifting, so the way the lift is carried out is assumed to affect the energy stored.
misconceptions.correction: None of the three quantities in Ep = m g h refers to time or speed, so the g.p.e. gained depends only on how heavy the object is and how high it is raised.

misconceptions.question: Does the value of g depend on the object being lifted?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is a property of the gravitational field, and its value is given in the question.
misconceptions.misconception: You work g out from the object, for example from its mass or from how high it is.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The letter g sits next to m and h in the equation, so it is assumed to be another property of the object being calculated from the data given.
misconceptions.correction: Gravitational field strength describes the field, not the object. In any calculation its value will be given.

misconceptions.question: In Ep = m g h, what does h mean?
misconceptions.correct: The vertical height the object is raised above ground level.
misconceptions.misconception: How tall the object itself is.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word height is used in everyday speech for the size of an object, so it is read as a property of the object rather than as a distance moved upwards.
misconceptions.correction: h is the height the object is raised above ground level. An object sitting on the ground gains no g.p.e. however tall it is.

mcqs.stem: A car of mass 1200 kg is travelling at a speed of 10 m/s. What is its kinetic energy?

options.rationale: Obtained by multiplying 0.5 × 1200 × 10, forgetting to square the speed.
Obtained from 1200 × 10², leaving out the factor of 0.5.
Obtained from 1200 × 10: both the 0.5 and the squaring have been dropped.

mcqs.stem: A cyclist rides at 4 m/s and then speeds up to 8 m/s. The mass of the cyclist and bicycle does not change. Compared with the kinetic energy at 4 m/s, the kinetic energy at 8 m/s is:

options.rationale: Chosen by treating kinetic energy as directly proportional to speed.
Speed is squared in Ek = 1/2 m v², so doubling v multiplies the kinetic energy by 2² = 4.
Chosen by cubing rather than squaring the factor of 2, a slip made when the index is misremembered.

options.text: the same as its old value
options.rationale: Chosen by students who believe the mass is what fixes the kinetic energy, and the mass has not changed.

mcqs.stem: Kinetic energy, elastic potential energy and gravitational potential energy are all measured in the same unit. Which unit is it?

options.rationale: Chosen by students who associate mechanics with the newton and treat it as the unit of energy.
Chosen by confusing energy with power, the rate at which energy is transferred.
All three energy stores in this section are measured in joules, J.
The unit of mass, which appears in two of the three equations and is easily picked out.

mcqs.stem: A student is about to substitute values into Ek = 1/2 m v². Which units must the quantities be in?

options.text: m in g and v in m/s
options.rationale: Chosen by students who substitute a mass given in grams without converting it.

options.text: m in N and v in m/s
options.rationale: Chosen by students who treat the newton as a unit of mass, confusing mass with weight.

options.text: m in kg and v in km/h
options.rationale: Chosen when the everyday unit for speed is used instead of the one the equation requires.

options.text: m in kg and v in m/s
options.rationale: The specification gives mass in kilograms, kg, and speed in metres per second, m/s, which give the kinetic energy in joules.

mcqs.stem: A ball of mass 250 g is moving at 4 m/s. What is its kinetic energy?

options.rationale: Obtained by substituting 250 for the mass without converting grams to kilograms.
Obtained from 0.5 × 0.25 × 4, with the speed not squared.
Obtained from 0.25 × 4², with the factor of 0.5 left out.

mcqs.stem: A spring with a spring constant of 200 N/m is stretched by 0.10 m, within its limit of proportionality. How much elastic potential energy is stored?

options.rationale: Obtained from 0.5 × 200 × 0.10, with the extension not squared.
Obtained from 200 × 0.10², with the factor of 0.5 left out.
Obtained from 200 × 0.10: both the 0.5 and the squaring have been dropped.

mcqs.stem: A spring with a spring constant of 50 N/m is stretched by 20 cm, within its limit of proportionality. How much elastic potential energy is stored?

options.rationale: Obtained by substituting 20 for the extension, so the answer is out by a factor of 100².
Obtained from 0.5 × 50 × 0.20, with the extension converted correctly but not squared.
Obtained from 0.5 × 50 × 20: the extension is neither converted nor squared.

mcqs.stem: A spring is stretched so far that its limit of proportionality is exceeded. What can now be said about using Ee = 1/2 k e² for that spring?

options.text: it still gives the energy stored exactly
options.rationale: Chosen by students who treat the bracketed condition as a footnote rather than a limit on when the equation works.

options.text: it gives the energy stored if k is doubled
options.rationale: Chosen by students who assume the spring simply takes a new spring constant beyond the limit.

options.text: it gives half of the energy stored
options.rationale: Chosen by students who expect a fixed numerical correction rather than a breakdown of the relationship.

options.text: it no longer gives the energy stored
options.rationale: The equation applies only while the limit of proportionality has not been exceeded, as the specification states.

mcqs.stem: In the equation Ee = 1/2 k e², the spring constant k is measured in which unit?

options.rationale: The specification gives the spring constant, k, in newtons per metre, N/m.
The unit of gravitational field strength, chosen because both constants are newtons per something.
Chosen by students who think the spring constant states the energy stored for each metre of extension.
The inverted unit, chosen when the extension and the force are the wrong way round.

mcqs.stem: In the equation Ep = m g h, the gravitational field strength g is measured in which unit?

options.rationale: The unit of the spring constant, chosen because the two constants are stored together.
The specification gives gravitational field strength, g, in newtons per kilogram, N/kg.
Chosen by students who read g as the energy each kilogram gains, because it sits inside an energy equation.
Chosen by students who think of gravity in terms of how fast objects fall.

mcqs.stem: A climber of mass 60 kg is raised 5.0 m up a cliff. The gravitational field strength is 9.8 N/kg. How much gravitational potential energy does the climber gain?

options.rationale: Obtained by including a factor of 0.5, carried across from the other two energy equations.
Obtained from 60 × 5.0, leaving the gravitational field strength out of the calculation.
Obtained from 60 × 9.8, which is the climber's weight rather than the energy gained.

mcqs.stem: A box of mass 20 kg is pushed 5.0 m along a ramp, which raises it 2.0 m vertically. The gravitational field strength is 10 N/kg. How much gravitational potential energy does the box gain?

options.rationale: Obtained by using the 5.0 m travelled along the ramp instead of the vertical height.
Obtained from 20 × 2.0, with the gravitational field strength left out of the calculation.
Obtained from 20 × 5.0, using the ramp distance and omitting g altogether.
h is the vertical height raised, so Ep = 20 × 10 × 2.0 = 400 J.

mcqs.stem: An object has a weight of 500 N at a place where the gravitational field strength is 10 N/kg. It is raised 3.0 m. How much gravitational potential energy does it gain?

options.rationale: Obtained by substituting the weight of 500 N as the mass.
Obtained from 50 × 3.0, with the gravitational field strength left out.
Obtained from 500 × 10, using the weight as the mass and leaving out the height.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is the equation for the gravitational potential energy gained by an object raised above ground level?

options.rationale: Chosen by carrying the factor of 0.5 across from the kinetic and elastic potential energy equations.
This is the equation as the specification states it: g.p.e. = mass × gravitational field strength × height.
Chosen by carrying the squared term across from the other two equations in this section.
Chosen by students who use weight and mass interchangeably.

mcqs.stem: An object of mass m is moving at speed v. Which expression gives its kinetic energy?

options.rationale: Chosen when the index is attached to the mass instead of the speed.
Chosen when the squared term is dropped from the recalled equation.
This is Ek = 1/2 m v², with the speed squared.
Chosen when the factor of 0.5 is treated as a minor correction and left out.

mcqs.stem: Which of these gives the elastic potential energy stored in a stretched spring, within the limit of proportionality?

options.rationale: Chosen when the squared term is attached to the spring constant rather than to the extension.
Chosen when the extension is not squared.
Chosen when the factor of 0.5 is left out of the equation.
This is the equation as the specification states it: Ee = 1/2 k e².

mcqs.stem: Object A has a mass of 4 kg and moves at 3 m/s. Object B has a mass of 2 kg and moves at 6 m/s. Comparing their kinetic energies:

options.text: B stores twice as much as A

options.rationale: Chosen because 4 × 3 and 2 × 6 are equal, comparing mass × speed instead of using the squared speed.

options.text: A stores twice as much as B
options.rationale: Chosen by students who assume the heavier object must store more energy.

options.text: B stores four times as much
options.rationale: Chosen by applying the four-times rule for doubled speed while ignoring the halved mass.

mcqs.stem: A question asks students to calculate the gravitational potential energy gained by a rock lifted onto a wall. Where does the value of the gravitational field strength come from?

options.text: it must be recalled as 10 N/kg
options.rationale: Chosen by students who have memorised a familiar value and assume it is always required.

options.text: it is given in the question
options.rationale: The specification states that in any calculation the value of the gravitational field strength (g) will be given.

options.text: it is calculated from the mass
options.rationale: Chosen by students who treat g as a property of the object rather than of the gravitational field.

options.text: it is worked out from the height
options.rationale: Chosen by students who assume g must be derived from the other data in the question.

mcqs.stem: A spring stores 0.90 J of elastic potential energy when its extension is 0.060 m, within the limit of proportionality. What is the spring constant?

options.rationale: Obtained from Ee / e², with the factor of 0.5 not carried through the rearrangement.
Obtained from Ee / e, with the extension not squared.
Rearranging Ee = 1/2 k e² gives k = 2Ee / e² = 1.8 / 0.0036 = 500 N/m.
Obtained from 2Ee / e, doubling correctly but not squaring the extension.

mcqs.stem: A crane lifts the same load to twice the height it lifted it before. Compared with the first lift, the gravitational potential energy gained is:

options.rationale: Chosen by carrying the squared relationship across from the kinetic energy equation.
Chosen by students who read h as the size of the load rather than the height it is raised.
Chosen when the relationship is inverted, as though raising a load higher were easier.
Height is not squared in Ep = m g h, so g.p.e. is directly proportional to height.
